provenance.task: Colony (not hive) insects as a distributed body: high-speed vs low-speed (stigmergic) communication between partitions; is stigmergy an externalized memory store?

findings.item: 1. SUPERORGANISM / DISTRIBUTED-BODY FRAMING — origin (Wheeler 1911)
findings.claim: The concept that a eusocial colony functions as one integrated organism (an 'organism' with division of labor as differentiated tissues/castes) was articulated by William Morton Wheeler in 'The ant-colony as an organism', Journal of Morphology 22:307-325 (1911). Wheeler treated the colony — not the individual ant — as the analog of the organism, with the reproductive caste as germ-line and workers as soma.
findings.citation: Wheeler, W.M. (1911). The ant-colony as an organism. Journal of Morphology 22(2):307-325. DOI 10.1002/jmor.1050220206. Verified via AntCat ref 130060, Journal of Morphology vol. 22 (1911), and PsycNet record 1911-10101-003.
findings.support: Pagination 307-325 and venue (J. Morphol. vol. 22, 1911) corroborated across three independent indexes (AntCat, UNSW embryology J. Morphol. v22 contents, PsycNet). Germ-line/soma framing restated in the modern Boomsma & Gawne 2018 review (which explicitly credits Wheeler's morphologically-differentiated-caste criterion).

findings.item: 1. SUPERORGANISM — modern synthesis (Hölldobler & Wilson 2009) + terminology
findings.claim: The superorganism framing was given its definitive modern synthesis in Hölldobler & Wilson, 'The Superorganism: The Beauty, Elegance, and Strangeness of Insect Societies' (2009). TERMINOLOGY as the task states is correct and standard: the COLONY (= superorganism) is the distributed organism; 'hive' refers specifically to the honey-bee NEST structure (the physical domicile), not the organism. ('Colony' is the organismal unit across ants, termites, and bees; 'hive' is bee-nest-specific.)
findings.citation: Hölldobler, B. & Wilson, E.O. (2009). The Superorganism: The Beauty, Elegance, and Strangeness of Insect Societies. New York: W.W. Norton. xxi+522 pp. ISBN 978-0-393-06704-0. Verified via W.W. Norton publisher page (9780393067040) and the Quarterly Review of Biology review (DOI 10.1086/650272, vol. 85 no. 1, 2010).
findings.support: ISBN, publisher, year, page count cross-checked across Norton, QRB review, and multiple booksellers. The colony-vs-hive terminological distinction is standard usage in the cited literature (von Frisch, Seeley, Hölldobler & Wilson) — 'hive' = bee domicile, 'colony' = the social unit; I did not find any source that uses 'hive' for ants/termites, consistent with the task's framing.

findings.item: 1. SUPERORGANISM — acceptance level + principal critiques
findings.claim: The superorganism framing is widely USED as an organizing heuristic but is CONTESTED as a strict evolutionary claim. After the 1960s rise of kin-selection/inclusive-fitness thinking it declined as a literal entity-level concept. Gardner & Grafen (2009) gave the first formal theory of group adaptation, concluding that between-group selection produces genuine superorganism-grade group adaptation only under restrictive conditions (effectively clonal/maximally-related groups; conflict-suppression mechanisms like policing are NOT themselves group adaptations). Boomsma & Gawne (2018) argue the loose ('sensu lato') superorganism concept is incorrect/uninformative and restrict true superorganismality to lineages with irreversible morphological caste differentiation (a 'point of no return' major evolutionary transition tied to lifetime monogamy / high relatedness).
findings.citation: Gardner, A. & Grafen, A. (2009). Capturing the superorganism: a formal theory of group adaptation. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 22(4):659-671. DOI 10.1111/j.1420-9101.2008.01681.x, PMID 19210588. — Boomsma, J.J. & Gawne, R. (2018). Superorganismality and caste differentiation as points of no return. Biological Reviews 93(1):28-54. DOI 10.1111/brv.12330, PMID 28508537.
findings.support: Both citations (authors/title/venue/vol/pages/DOI/PMID) verified at Oxford Academic / Wiley / PubMed. The broader kin-selection-vs-group-selection controversy (e.g., Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson 2010 in Nature, which attacked inclusive-fitness theory and drew a large rebuttal) is the well-documented backdrop; I verified the Gardner & Grafen and Boomsma critiques directly but did NOT re-verify the Nowak-Tarnita-Wilson Nature paper at source in this pass, so I flag that one as cited-but-not-reverified.

findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — antennation (antennal contact)
findings.claim: Antennation is direct antenna-to-body contact between adjacent individuals; it is the read step for cuticular-hydrocarbon (CHC) nestmate-recognition and task-allocation cues, operating on a sub-second-to-seconds, transient basis. It is RECIPROCAL/bidirectional in the sense that contact is mutual physical assay (each ant can evaluate the other's CHC profile on contact), and colony-wide contact rates oscillate (~3-4 peaks/hour) shaping information transmission.
findings.citation: Richardson, T.O. et al. (2017). Short-term activity cycles impede information transmission in ant colonies. PLOS Computational Biology 13(5):e1005527. DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005527 (PMC5443549). CHC-via-antennal-contact recognition: see e.g. Esponda & Gordon (2015) 'Distributed nestmate recognition in ants', Proc. R. Soc. B (PMC4426612).
findings.support: Contact-rate oscillation (~3-4 peaks/hr) and antennal-contact CHC assay verified via PLOS Comp Biol and the distributed-recognition literature. 'Sub-second to seconds' per-contact duration is the standard characterization but I did not pin a single primary source giving a precise per-antennation contact duration in milliseconds — flagged as a quantitative gap. 'Reciprocal' here means mutual physical assay, not necessarily a signal-and-answer exchange.

findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — trophallaxis (fluid exchange carrying chemical + information)
findings.claim: Trophallaxis is mouth-to-mouth (stomodeal) fluid exchange between adjacent individuals — a direct, contact-based channel. LeBoeuf et al. (2016) showed the exchanged oral fluid carries far more than food: in the ant Camponotus floridanus it contains specific proteins, hydrocarbons, microRNAs, and the developmental regulator juvenile hormone, so trophallaxis constitutes a private, network-forming CHEMICAL-INFORMATION channel linking every colony member and influencing collective development. It is inherently bidirectional/reciprocal (a donor-recipient dyadic exchange) though the informational payload (e.g., JH) flows donor-to-recipient.
findings.citation: LeBoeuf, A.C., Waridel, P., Brent, C.S., Gonçalves, A.N., Menin, L., Ortiz, D., Riba-Grognuz, O., Koto, A., Soares, Z.G., Privman, E., Miska, E.A., Benton, R. & Keller, L. (2016). Oral transfer of chemical cues, growth proteins and hormones in social insects. eLife 5:e20375. DOI 10.7554/eLife.20375, PMID 27894417 (PMC5153251).
findings.support: Citation verified at eLife / PubMed. NOTE the task framed trophallaxis with honeybees as an example, but the LeBoeuf primary study is in the ANT Camponotus floridanus; the JH/protein/miRNA payload finding is attributed to that ant. Trophallaxis as food-and-fluid exchange is general across ants, bees, termites; the specific 'information network' payload claim is best-attested in the ant. Per-event timescale is seconds; I did not pin an exact mean duration at source.

findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — termite vibrational / substrate-borne signals (head-banging / drumming)
findings.claim: Disturbed termite soldiers (and workers) drum the head against the substrate, producing pulse-train substrate-borne vibrational ALARM signals. In Macrotermes natalensis pulse-train signals propagate at ~130 m/s along nest galleries (attenuating ~0.4 dB/cm) for long-distance alarm; pulse repetition rates ~13-26 Hz (M. subhyalinus ~13 Hz, M. bellicosus ~26 Hz). The channel is fast/transient and shows RECIPROCAL relay/positive-feedback: receivers respond by escaping AND by themselves head-banging, propagating the signal (a closed-loop, answered-by-another's-signal structure).
findings.citation: Hager, F.A. & Kirchner, W.H. (2013). Vibrational long-distance communication in the termites Macrotermes natalensis and Odontotermes sp. Journal of Experimental Biology 216(17):3249-3256. DOI 10.1242/jeb.083295, PMID 23926309. (Reticulitermes head-rebound ~4 ms detail and earlier Macrotermes alarm-physics work corroborate.)
findings.support: Propagation velocity (~130 m/s), attenuation (~0.4 dB/cm), pulse rates, and the relay/positive-feedback (receivers re-drum) verified via JEB abstract/PubMed. The relay behavior is the clearest documented RECIPROCAL/closed-loop structure in this catalog.

findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — honeybee stop-signal (inhibitory, answered) and vibration/shaking signal
findings.claim: The honeybee STOP-signal is a brief vibrational pulse delivered by head-butting a waggle-dancer, inhibiting/halting her dancing — an explicitly RECIPROCAL, closed-loop, signal-elicits-response interaction. Nieh (2010) showed foragers that meet danger at a feeder return and deliver stop-signals to dancers advertising that site (negative feedback curbing recruitment). The DVAV/vibration ('shaking') signal (Schneider & Lewis work; ~18 Hz, ~1-1.4 s bouts) non-specifically raises recipient activity. Both are sub-second-to-seconds, transient, direct between adjacent bees.
findings.citation: Nieh, J.C. (2010). A negative feedback signal that is triggered by peril curbs honey bee recruitment. Current Biology 20(4):310-315. DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2009.12.060. — DVAV/vibration signal: Schneider, S.S. & Lewis, L.A. (2004) review of the vibration signal (Apidologie); house-hunting DVAV ~18.05±0.45 Hz for 1.36±0.23 s per Visscher/Lewis-lineage work.
findings.support: Nieh 2010 (Current Biology 20:310-315) verified. The stop-signal's reciprocal/answered structure is its defining feature and is the cleanest 'closed-loop edge' in the bee literature. DVAV frequency/duration figures verified via the long-term DVAV characterization (Sci. Rep. 2018, PMC6167329) and house-hunting DVAV work; I did not re-verify the exact Schneider & Lewis Apidologie page numbers at source, so that specific cite is flagged thin.

findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — fast volatile alarm pheromones (rapid release + rapid decay)
findings.claim: Sting alarm pheromone in Apis mellifera — chiefly isopentyl/isoamyl acetate (IPA), synthesized near the sting (Koschevnikov gland) — is rapidly released on disturbance and is the most volatile component, triggering fast colony defensive recruitment. It functions as a near-instantaneous, transient, broadcast-to-nearby-nestmates signal. Whether it is reciprocal is largely ONE-WAY release-and-respond rather than an answered dyadic exchange (responders may release their own alarm pheromone, giving a positive-feedback amplification rather than a targeted reply).
findings.citation: Alarm-pheromone identity/volatility: e.g. Boch, R., Shearer, D.A. & Stone, B.C. (1962) Nature 195:1018-1020 (identification of isoamyl acetate as honeybee alarm pheromone); volatility ranking discussed in modern reviews (e.g. alarm-pheromone eavesdropping work, PMC4860575).
findings.support: The IDENTITY (IPA / isoamyl acetate as principal sting alarm pheromone) and its HIGH VOLATILITY are well-established and were corroborated across multiple secondary sources, but I could NOT pin a primary source giving a quantified decay/half-life IN SECONDS for IPA in this pass, and I did not re-verify the classic Boch et al. 1962 Nature citation at source. FLAG: the 'rapid decay quantified' part of the task is thin/single-source-weak. Treat the seconds-scale decay as qualitatively asserted, not quantitatively attested.

findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — trail pheromones (deposition, persistence/half-life, reinforcement)
findings.claim: Trail pheromones are deposited on the substrate (WRITTEN by depositing ants) and FOLLOWED later by nestmates (READ), persisting minutes-to-much-longer with positive-feedback reinforcement (more traffic -> more deposition -> stronger trail) and negative-feedback / no-entry signals. Persistence is highly species- and substrate-dependent: Pharaoh ant (Monomorium pharaonis) trails lose ~50% efficacy in ~3 minutes on paper (volatile faranal), whereas Oecophylla longinoda trail marks remained detectable for weeks. Czaczkes, Grüter & Ratnieks (2015) give the integrative review: trails regulate foraging via positive AND negative feedback and are complementary/synergistic with individual memory.
findings.citation: Czaczkes, T.J., Grüter, C. & Ratnieks, F.L.W. (2015). Trail pheromones: an integrative view of their role in social insect colony organization. Annual Review of Entomology 60:581-599. DOI 10.1146/annurev-ento-010814-020627. — Pharaoh-ant decay: Jeanson, R., Ratnieks, F.L.W. & Deneubourg, J.-L. (2003). Pheromone trail decay rates on different substrates in the Pharaoh's ant, Monomorium pharaonis. Physiological Entomology 28(3):192-198. DOI 10.1046/j.1365-3032.2003.00332.x. — Trail-pheromone-identity catalog: Cerdá, X. et al. (2014) Natural Product Communications 9(8).
findings.support: Czaczkes et al. 2015 (Annu. Rev. Entomol. 60:581-599) and Jeanson et al. 2003 (Physiol. Entomol., Pharaoh ant ~50% efficacy in ~3 min on paper) verified at venue. The species-range of persistence (minutes to weeks) is well-documented. Reinforcement (positive feedback) is the canonical mechanism (Camazine et al. 2001; Czaczkes 2015).

findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — STIGMERGY as organizing principle (Grassé 1959; Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999)
findings.claim: Grassé (1959) coined 'stigmergie' from termite nest-(re)construction: the work already accomplished (a soil pellet, a pillar) stimulates the next act, so coordination is mediated by the modified ENVIRONMENT, not by direct worker-to-worker instruction ('stimulation of workers by the performance they have achieved'). Theraulaz & Bonabeau (1999) formalized it and distinguished quantitative vs qualitative stigmergy; it underpins the broader swarm-intelligence synthesis (Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz). It is the LOW-SPEED, INDIRECT, environment-mediated, one-to-many-across-time channel.
findings.citation: Grassé, P.-P. (1959). La reconstruction du nid et les coordinations interindividuelles chez Bellicositermes natalensis et Cubitermes sp. La théorie de la stigmergie: essai d'interprétation du comportement des termites constructeurs. Insectes Sociaux 6(1):41-80. DOI 10.1007/BF02223791. — Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (1999). A brief history of stigmergy. Artificial Life 5(2):97-116. DOI 10.1162/106454699568700, PMID 10633572.
findings.support: Grassé 1959 (Insectes Sociaux vol. 6, ~pp. 41-80/81; sources vary slightly on end page 80 vs 81 — minor) and Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999 (Artif. Life 5(2):97-116, PMID 10633572) both verified at venue/PubMed. Swarm-intelligence synthesis (Bonabeau, Dorigo, Theraulaz 1999 'Swarm Intelligence', Oxford Univ. Press) is the standard formalization reference but I did not re-verify that book at source this pass.

findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — nest/structure construction as environmentally-stored template; queen pheromone & CHC colony-identity field
findings.claim: Built nest structures are environmentally-stored templates: the partially-built structure encodes what the next builder does (stigmergic construction), persisting hours-to-days-to-the-colony-lifetime. Separately, queen pheromone and the colony's cuticular-hydrocarbon (CHC) profile constitute a persistent chemical IDENTITY field read by nestmates (recognition, reproductive regulation). Notably, recognition cues can be deposited INTO and re-acquired FROM the shared nest material itself — nest soil mediates indirect transfer of recognition cues between nestmates — a stigmergic identity-field mechanism.
findings.citation: Stigmergic construction templates: Camazine, S., Deneubourg, J.-L., Franks, N.R., Sneyd, J., Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (2001). Self-Organization in Biological Systems. Princeton Univ. Press. ISBN 978-0-691-11624-2. — Nest-material recognition-cue transfer: 'Wax On, Wax Off: Nest Soil Facilitates Indirect Transfer of Recognition Cues between Ant Nestmates' (PLoS ONE, PMC3084846).
findings.support: Camazine et al. 2001 (Princeton, ISBN verified) is the canonical self-organization/stigmergic-construction reference. The nest-soil recognition-cue-transfer paper is verified at PMC (PMC3084846) and directly supports the 'identity field written into the shared medium' framing. Queen-pheromone regulation is well-established generally; I did not pin a single primary queen-pheromone citation at source this pass — flagged as relying on the general literature.

findings.item: 3. LOAD-BEARING QUESTION — is stigmergy treated as EXTERNALIZED, ENVIRONMENTALLY-STORED MEMORY?
findings.claim: YES — the literature explicitly frames the pheromone field / built structure as an externalized collective memory written by some individuals and read by others displaced in time, distinct from any single nervous system. Hunt, Franks & Baddeley (2020) state plainly: 'One way to circumvent the cost of carrying memories internally is to store the information externally in the environment,' and show Temnothorax albipennis ants converge on optimal exploration faster when prior chemical marks accumulate (uncleaned arena, p=0.0161) — framing the shared substrate as an 'external memory store' and the colony as a Bayesian superorganism. The terms 'collective memory', 'external/externalized memory', and 'stigmergic memory' are used in the primary collective-behavior literature; the broader 'extended cognition / extended mind' reading is imported from philosophy of mind (Clark & Chalmers 1998) and is more metaphorical/interpretive when applied to colonies.
findings.citation: Hunt, E.R., Franks, N.R. & Baddeley, R.J. (2020). The Bayesian superorganism: externalized memories facilitate distributed sampling. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 17(167):20190848. DOI 10.1098/rsif.2019.0848. (Extended-mind philosophical frame: Clark, A. & Chalmers, D. (1998). The extended mind. Analysis 58(1):7-19.)
findings.support: Hunt, Franks & Baddeley 2020 verified at J. R. Soc. Interface, with the exact 'store the information externally in the environment' framing and the p=0.0161 result confirmed via the article. ESTABLISHED vs METAPHORICAL distinction: 'external/collective/stigmergic memory' is an established, operationally-defined usage in this primary source (the environment measurably stores route/exploration information read back later); 'extended cognition/extended mind' is the more contested, philosophical extension (Clark & Chalmers cited as the source frame, not re-verified at source this pass).

findings.item: 4. SYNTHESIS — does the high-speed/low-speed split hold, and the waggle-dance blur
findings.claim: The two-channel (latency) organization is a robust ORGANIZING distinction but BLURS at the edges, most sharply with the honeybee WAGGLE DANCE: it is a high-speed, direct, point-to-small-group channel (a dancer signals a handful of nearby followers in real time) that nonetheless ENCODES PERSISTENT SPATIAL information (direction via angle-to-gravity; distance via waggle-run duration, ~75 ms per ~100 m, i.e. ~1 s waggle run ≈ ~1 km). So a fast channel carries map-like content that a stigmergic field would otherwise hold. Vibrational signals (stop-signal, DVAV) further blur it by MODULATING the slower recruitment/decision dynamics. The split is by LATENCY (transient direct contact vs persistent environmental store), not by information-type.
findings.citation: Waggle-dance distance/direction encoding: von Frisch, K. (1967). The Dance Language and Orientation of Bees. Cambridge, MA: Belknap/Harvard Univ. Press. (~75 ms per 100 m relation; angle-to-gravity direction encoding.) Stop-signal cross-inhibition coupling fast signals to collective decisions: Seeley et al. (2012) Science 335(6064):108-111.
findings.support: von Frisch 1967 (Belknap/Harvard) verified as the canonical dance-language reference; the ~75 ms/100 m and angle-to-gravity encoding are standard textbook values (corroborated across multiple sources, though the exact slope is non-linear and optic-flow-calibrated). The waggle dance as a fast-channel-carrying-persistent-spatial-info is the literature's own recognized tension, not solely the researcher's imposition.

findings.item: 4. SYNTHESIS — ranking the three taxa by clean latency separation
findings.claim: Ranking by how CLEANLY the two channels separate by latency (cleanest first): (1) TERMITES — sharpest separation: fast = substrate-borne vibrational drumming (ms-pulse-train alarm, relayed); slow = the constructed mound/nest itself (the founding stigmergy case, Grassé 1959), persisting for the colony's lifetime; little 'fast channel carrying a spatial map' confound. (2) ANTS — clean but with overlap: fast = antennation/trophallaxis/vibration; slow = trail-pheromone field + CHC identity field as external memory (Hunt et al. 2020); the trail field straddles minutes-to-weeks. (3) HONEY BEES — most BLURRED: the waggle dance is a fast channel that carries persistent spatial content, and stop/vibration signals modulate slow collective decisions, so latency and information-type cross over. This ranking is partly the researcher's imposition; the literature does not present an explicit cross-taxon latency ranking.
findings.citation: Synthesis across: Grassé 1959 (Insectes Sociaux 6:41-80) [termite construction]; Hunt, Franks & Baddeley 2020 (J. R. Soc. Interface 17:20190848) [ant external memory]; von Frisch 1967 & Seeley et al. 2012 (Science 335:108-111) [bee dance/stop-signal blur]; Czaczkes, Grüter & Ratnieks 2015 (Annu. Rev. Entomol. 60:581-599) [trail-field timescales].
findings.support: Each component citation is individually verified above. The RANKING itself is a defensible synthesis built from those sources but is NOT a claim any single cited author makes as a cross-taxon ordering — explicitly flagged as the researcher's organizing imposition, not the organism's documented self-description. Where the literature is silent: no source I found ranks termites/ants/bees by latency-channel separation, so confidence on the ordering is medium.

opus_survey.cross_cutting:
TERMINOLOGY (verified consistent with the cited literature): 'colony' / 'superorganism' = the distributed organismal unit (ants, termites, honey bees); 'hive' = the honey-bee NEST structure specifically, never the organism and not used for ants/termites. This matches the task's framing and the usage in von Frisch, Seeley, and Hölldobler & Wilson.

TWO-CHANNEL ORGANIZATION (the spine of the dive), stated as a latency partition the literature SUPPORTS but does not itself name as a binary: (A) HIGH-SPEED / DIRECT / POINT-TO-POINT, sub-second-to-seconds, transient, between adjacent (air-gapped) bodies — antennation, trophallaxis, substrate-borne vibration (termite drumming; bee stop-signal & DVAV), fast volatile alarm pheromone. Reciprocity grades from clearly CLOSED-LOOP/answered (bee stop-signal halts a specific dancer; termite drumming is relayed by receivers) through mutual-assay (antennation, trophallaxis dyad) to largely ONE-WAY release-and-amplify (alarm pheromone). (B) LOW-SPEED / INDIRECT / STIGMERGIC, minutes-to-hours-to-colony-lifetime, broadcast one-to-many across time, mediated by the SHARED ENVIRONMENT — trail-pheromone fields (written by deposition, read by following, reinforced by traffic), the built nest/mound (Grassé's founding stigmergy case), and the queen-pheromone / cuticular-hydrocarbon colony-identity field (which can be written into and re-read from the nest material itself).

THE LOAD-BEARING QUESTION resolves AFFIRMATIVELY in the primary literature: stigmergy IS treated as externalized, environmentally-stored memory. Hunt, Franks & Baddeley (2020, J. R. Soc. Interface) state it operationally ('store the information externally in the environment'; the shared substrate as an 'external memory store'), with a measured effect (faster optimal convergence with accumulated marks, p=0.0161). 'Collective/external/stigmergic memory' is ESTABLISHED, operationally-defined usage; 'extended cognition / extended mind' (Clark & Chalmers frame) is the more METAPHORICAL/contested extension.

SUPERORGANISM STATUS: widely USED heuristic, CONTESTED as a strict entity-level evolutionary claim — Wheeler 1911 origin; Hölldobler & Wilson 2009 modern synthesis; Gardner & Grafen 2009 formal limits; Boomsma & Gawne 2018 restriction to irreversible-caste 'points of no return'; the broader kin-vs-group-selection controversy (Nowak-Tarnita-Wilson 2010) is the backdrop.

THE SPLIT BLURS, primarily at the honeybee waggle dance — a FAST direct channel that nonetheless encodes PERSISTENT spatial map-content (~75 ms/100 m; angle-to-gravity) — so the partition is by LATENCY (transient direct edge vs persistent environmental store), NOT by information-type. Cleanest-to-blurriest latency separation: termites > ants > honey bees (this ordering is the researcher's synthesis, not any cited author's explicit claim).

CITATION INTEGRITY: every load-bearing source was verified at its venue/index this pass (authors+title+venue+year+vol/pages+DOI/PMID/ISBN). All primary citations are OA or textbook/index-verifiable (no reliance on paywalled-only DOIs for the claims). Items I did NOT re-verify at source and flagged accordingly: Nowak-Tarnita-Wilson 2010 (Nature), Boch et al. 1962 (Nature, alarm-pheromone ID), Bonabeau/Dorigo/Theraulaz 1999 'Swarm Intelligence' (Oxford), Clark & Chalmers 1998 'The extended mind', and the exact Schneider & Lewis Apidologie pagination — these are cited from corroborating secondary sources and named as not-reverified.
opus_survey.uncentered_note: FRAMEWORK LENS — offered ONLY as a reading, NOT a claim any cited author makes: the colony can be read as a MACRO-SCALE, HUMAN-LATENCY, DIRECTLY-OBSERVABLE instance of a distributed store/retrieve action — the high-speed direct channel as the transient reciprocal EDGE between air-gapped bodies (antennation/trophallaxis/vibration/stop-signal), the low-speed stigmergic channel as the PERSISTENT STORE externalized into the shared medium (sculpt = deposit pheromone / build structure; read = follow / respond later) — the same store/retrieve cascade that cellular substrates (bioelectric Vmem patterns, RNA, synaptic webs) run invisibly, here made watchable and cataloggable at human timescale. This is a LENS, not biology: the cited authors describe stigmergy, externalized memory, and direct signaling on their own terms (Grassé's coordination-via-modified-environment; Hunt et al.'s 'external memory store'; Nieh's negative-feedback stop-signal); they do NOT assert a unified store/retrieve cascade or any cross-substrate (cellular/colony) identity. UNCENTERING DISCIPLINE: I privileged no single taxon — the catalog holds ants, termites, and honey bees in parallel, and I named explicitly where centering on honey bees (the most-studied, most-anthropomorphized) would HIDE fiber-content (the waggle-dance blur is a bee artifact; termites show the cleanest latency separation; the ant trail-field is the clearest external-memory demonstration). No A-N cascade, Klein-4, or srmech operation is asserted as established biology here; the framework reading is held alongside, never substituted for, the literature's own assertions.
gaps: Honeybee alarm-pheromone (isoamyl/isopentyl acetate) DECAY/half-life in seconds was NOT pinned to a primary source this pass — identity and high volatility are well-established, but the quantitative 'rapid decay' figure is thin/single-source-weak. The classic Boch, Shearer & Stone 1962 Nature identification was cited from secondary corroboration, not re-verified at source.

Per-event TIMESCALES for antennation and trophallaxis (precise contact durations in ms/seconds) were not pinned to a single primary source; characterized qualitatively as sub-second-to-seconds from the general literature.

RECIPROCITY of trophallaxis is dyadic exchange, but the directionality of the INFORMATIONAL payload (e.g., juvenile hormone flowing donor->recipient) vs the bidirectional fluid exchange is a subtlety the primary source (LeBoeuf 2016) frames around development, not a symmetric 'signal-and-answer' loop — do not overstate it as closed-loop.
Queen-pheromone colony-identity-field claim relies on the general literature; no single primary queen-pheromone citation was pinned at source this pass.

The cross-taxon LATENCY-SEPARATION RANKING (termites > ants > bees) is a synthesis/imposition by the researcher; NO cited author presents such an explicit ordering, and the literature is effectively silent on a formal cross-taxon comparison of channel-latency cleanliness. Confidence medium.

Not re-verified at source this pass (cited from corroborating secondary sources, flagged): Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson 2010 (Nature, kin-selection controversy); Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz 1999 'Swarm Intelligence' (Oxford Univ. Press); Clark & Chalmers 1998 'The extended mind' (Analysis 58:7-19); exact Schneider & Lewis DVAV Apidologie pagination.
Grassé 1959 end-page is reported as 80 vs 81 across indexes (Insectes Sociaux vol. 6, starting p. 41) — minor pagination ambiguity, does not affect the attestation.

findings.item: Superorganism framing — Wheeler 1911 foundational paper
findings.claim: William Morton Wheeler (1911) coined the functional superorganism framing in 'The ant-colony as an organism,' Journal of Morphology, vol. 22, pp. 307–325. He argued that a colony meets the criteria of biological individuality: it acts as a cohesive unit, persists over time, undergoes development, and — because of reproductive division of labor — is the reproducing unit of selection. He drew an analogy between worker/soldier castes and somatic tissues, with the queen as the reproductive germ-line.
findings.citation: Wheeler, W.M. (1911). The ant-colony as an organism. Journal of Morphology, 22, 307–325. Verified via AntCat reference database (antcat.org/references/130060) and PsycNET record (psycnet.apa.org/record/1911-10101-003). No DOI for this 1911 paper; bibliographic details confirmed at both sources.

findings.item: Superorganism framing — Hölldobler & Wilson 2009 monograph
findings.claim: Hölldobler, B. & Wilson, E.O. (2009). The Superorganism: The Beauty, Elegance, and Strangeness of Insect Societies. W.W. Norton & Company, New York. This book-length treatment revived and updated the superorganism concept within contemporary sociobiology, framing the colony as an integrated organism whose organization emerges from feedback loops among local interactions rather than hierarchical command. The authors also authored the Pulitzer Prize–winning 'The Ants' (1990, Harvard University Press / Springer), a primary reference on ant communication chemistry.
findings.citation: Hölldobler, B. & Wilson, E.O. (2009). The Superorganism. W.W. Norton, New York. ISBN 978-0-393-06704-0. Confirmed via PMC article (PMC6901679) which cites the publisher directly. 'The Ants' (1990, Springer Berlin, 732 pp) confirmed via Oxford Academic review doi:10.1093/jeb/5.1.169.

findings.item: Superorganism framing — acceptance and principal critiques
findings.claim: The superorganism concept is widely used in collective-behavior and social-insect biology but carries three recognized critiques: (1) Post-1960s gene-centered biology disfavored it as group-selectionist; it was revived after multi-level selection theory was rehabilitated. (2) The 2010 Nowak–Tarnita–Wilson paper (Nature 466: 1057–1062, doi:10.1038/nature09205) challenged kin-selection/inclusive-fitness explanations for eusociality, provoking a major debate (over 130 researchers signed a rebuttal in Nature 471: E1–E4, 2011), showing the evolutionary framing of the superorganism remains contested — though this debate concerns the evolutionary origin of eusociality, not the descriptive superorganism framing itself. (3) A 2019 Frontiers in Psychology review (PMC6901679, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02653) notes that the mainstream claim that 'hierarchical control does not occur' may underweight Wheeler's original physiological emphasis. The terminology 'hive' = the honey-bee nest structure specifically (not the organism) is standard in beekeeping and entomology; 'colony' or 'superorganism' = the distributed organism.
findings.citation: Nowak, M.A., Tarnita, C.E. & Wilson, E.O. (2010). The evolution of eusociality. Nature, 466, 1057–1062. doi:10.1038/nature09205. Frontiers/PMC review: Witkowski, O. & Ikegami, T. (2019). Revising the Superorganism. Front. Psychol. 10:2653. PMC6901679. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02653.

findings.item: High-speed channel — antennation: rate, timescale, bidirectionality
findings.claim: Antennation (antennal contact between two individuals) operates at 19.5–41.5 antenna strikes per second in Odontomachus trap-jaw ants, measured by high-speed videography. The behavior is so rapid it is invisible to the human eye without high-speed video. The interaction is reciprocal: both participants drum each other's antennae simultaneously or in rapid alternation, making it a bidirectional closed-loop exchange. In Reznikova & Ryabko's maze studies (Formica polyctena), the time spent antennating was proportional to the information content (number of maze branches to convey), suggesting the channel carries structured, quantifiable information at sub-second-to-seconds timescales per interaction bout.
findings.citation: O'Fallon, S., Suarez, A.V. & Smith, A.A. (2016). A comparative analysis of rapid antennation behavior in four species of Odontomachus trap-jaw ants. Insectes Sociaux, 63(3), 409–417. doi:10.1007/s00040-016-0462-6. Reznikova, Z. & Ryabko, B. (1988). Experimental proof of the use of numerals in the language of ants. Problemy Peredachi Informatsii, 24(4), 80–86. NOTE: The Reznikova 1988 citation is attested through secondary review (Myrmecological News Blog 2018-06-22; Reznikova's own website reznikova.net); the original 1988 Russian-language paper has not been directly fetched — FLAG: treat as single-source indirect.

findings.item: High-speed channel — trophallaxis: timescale, bidirectionality, information content
findings.claim: Trophallaxis (mouth-to-mouth fluid exchange) operates over seconds to minutes per event (mean inter-event interval ~240 ± 17 s in Camponotus). Events themselves are brief (seconds to tens of seconds). While the primary function is food transfer, trophallactic fluid contains cuticular hydrocarbons, microRNAs, juvenile hormone, and growth-regulatory proteins — making each event a compound chemical information transfer. The interaction involves antennation throughout (both individuals antennate during the exchange), rendering it bidirectional in the signaling layer even when food flow is one-directional. Rare role-reversal events (donor↔receiver) confirm the channel is not strictly unidirectional. LeBoeuf et al. (2016) showed that a single trophallaxis event transfers ~31 picograms of juvenile hormone — 5–31% of a third-instar larva's total JH content — with measurable developmental consequences (doubled metamorphosis success rate), demonstrating functional-level information transfer.
findings.citation: Greenwald, E., Segre, E. & Feinerman, O. (2015). Ant trophallactic networks: simultaneous measurement of interaction patterns and food dissemination. Scientific Reports, 5, 12496. PMID 26224025. doi:10.1038/srep12496. LeBoeuf, A.C., Waridel, P., Brent, C.S. et al. (2016). Oral transfer of chemical cues, growth proteins and hormones in social insects. eLife, 5, e20375. PMID 27894417. doi:10.7554/eLife.20375.

findings.item: High-speed channel — termite vibrational alarm: timescale, unidirectionality, relay mechanism
findings.claim: Termites produce substrate-borne alarm signals by head-banging (vertical oscillatory movement against tunnel walls), generating pulse trains at 10–20 Hz. In Macrotermes natalensis and Odontotermes sp., the physical wave propagates at ~130 m/s through galleries but attenuates ~0.4 dB/cm, limiting direct-wave range to ~0.4 m per source. Individual soldiers respond within ~0.3 s (sub-second reaction time) by drumming themselves, creating relay chains that propagate alarm across the colony at ~1.3 m/s (M. natalensis) to ~2.1 m/s (Odontotermes sp.) without signal decrement over several meters. This relay mechanism is fundamentally one-way broadcast (alarm→flee/attack): workers retreat toward nest, soldiers advance toward disturbance. Positive feedback between pheromone release and vibrational drumming intensifies the signal, but the propagation is not a closed-loop dialogue.
findings.citation: Hager, F.A. & Kirchner, W.H. (2013). Vibrational long-distance communication in the termites Macrotermes natalensis and Odontotermes sp. Journal of Experimental Biology, 216(17), 3249–3256. doi:10.1242/jeb.086991. Verified by direct fetch of the journal article.

findings.item: High-speed channel — honeybee stop signal: frequency, duration, directionality
findings.claim: The honeybee stop signal (also called the inhibitory signal) is a 302–550 Hz vibrational pulse (~150–258 ms duration per pulse) delivered by a worker head-butting the body of a waggle dancer or departing forager. Tan et al. (2016) showed signals during large hornet nest attacks produce pulses at ~550 Hz and ~258 ms, while forager attack contexts produce ~502 Hz and ~178 ms. The stop signal is strictly one-directional (one bee delivers → receiver freezes momentarily); receivers do not reciprocate with their own stop signals. The signal serves two functions: foraging inhibition (dangerous food sources) and colony alarm (prevents departure when nest is threatened). Response is immediate (receiver freezes during delivery), though precise millisecond latency is not quantified in the cited study.
findings.citation: Tan, K., Dong, S., Li, X. et al. (2016). Honey Bee Inhibitory Signaling Is Tuned to Threat Severity and Can Act as a Colony Alarm Signal. PLOS Biology, 14(3), e1002423. doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002423. PMC4807812. Verified by direct fetch of the PMC full text.

findings.item: High-speed channel — honeybee waggle dance: spatial encoding, fast delivery, point-to-small-group
findings.claim: The waggle dance (Karl von Frisch, Nobel Prize 1973; confirmed experimentally by Riley et al. 2005 in Nature) encodes food-source direction (waggle-run angle relative to vertical = sun azimuth) and distance (waggle-run duration; ~2.5 s waggle run ≈ 2,625 m). Each dance circuit takes seconds; followers attend multiple circuits to average the information. The communication is point-to-small-group (dancer to a few attending followers), delivered at human-observable speed (seconds per circuit, minutes per recruitment bout). Crucially, the dance encodes SPATIAL information (a vector: direction + distance) into a real-time kinematic signal — the dance itself lasts only while performed and is not externally stored. However, the dancer relies on a persisting internal memory of the food-source location to produce the dance; the dance itself is transient. The information encoded (spatial vector to a distant resource) is PERSISTENT in type but the channel is TRANSIENT in mechanism. This is the 'bridge case' described in Question 4: a high-speed direct channel that encodes what would otherwise be stigmergic information.
findings.citation: von Frisch, K. (1967). The Dance Language and Orientation of Bees. Harvard University Press (Nobel Lecture 1973: nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/frisch-lecture.pdf). Riley, J.R. et al. (2005). The flight paths of honeybees recruited by the waggle dance. Nature, 435, 205–207. doi:10.1038/nature03526. FLAG: the 2005 Riley et al. DOI is confirmed via search but not direct-fetched.

findings.item: High-speed channel — volatile alarm pheromones: rapid release, rapid decay
findings.claim: Isoamyl acetate (isopentyl acetate) is the primary sting-alarm pheromone component in honeybees (Apis mellifera); it is highly volatile, causing rapid dispersal and quick decay from the active space. Alarm pheromones in ants (e.g., fire ant Solenopsis invicta: alkylpyrazine released from mandibular glands) similarly act at seconds-to-minutes timescales before the active concentration drops below the behavioral threshold. Specific half-life measurements in field conditions were not recovered in this search for these volatile alarm compounds — FLAG: quantified half-life data for isoamyl acetate or fire ant alarm pheromone active-space decay is not attested to a directly-verified primary source here; the fast-decay property is described qualitatively in multiple sources but precise kinetic values require specialist chemistry literature (e.g., Bossert & Wilson 1963 active-space model).
findings.citation: Alarm pheromone identification: Boch, R., Shearer, D.A. & Stone, B.C. (1962). Identification of isoamyl acetate as an active component in the sting pheromone of the honey bee. Nature, 195, 1018–1020. doi:10.1038/1951018a0. EAG studies: MDPI Insects 2019, 10(11), 403. doi:10.3390/insects10110403. PMC6920760. FLAG: the Boch et al. 1962 DOI is confirmed via search (ScienceDirect listing) but not direct-fetched; treat as attested via secondary corroboration only.

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — Grassé 1959: coin of the concept and mechanism
findings.claim: Pierre-Paul Grassé (1959) coined 'stigmergie' in studying termite nest reconstruction in Bellicositermes natalensis and Cubitermes sp. The paper, 'La reconstruction du nid et les coordinations inter-individuelles chez Bellicositermes natalensis et Cubitermes sp. La théorie de la stigmergie,' was published in Insectes Sociaux, vol. 6, pp. 41–81. Grassé's core observation: termites are NOT responding to each other directly when building; they are responding to the structure already built. A pellet deposited at a location stimulates the next termite to deposit there, creating pillars and arches without any individual holding a blueprint. The MEDIUM (the growing structure, possibly impregnated with pheromone) is what carries the coordinating information forward in time.
findings.citation: Grassé, P.-P. (1959). La reconstruction du nid et les coordinations inter-individuelles chez Bellicositermes natalensis et Cubitermes sp. La théorie de la stigmergie: Essai d'interprétation du comportement des termites constructeurs. Insectes Sociaux, 6(1), 41–81. doi:10.1007/BF02223791 (confirmed via Springer Nature Link listing; article page fetched indirectly via Semantic Scholar). Confirmed: volume 6, pp. 41–81, year 1959, journal Insectes Sociaux.

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999: formal history and definition
findings.claim: Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (1999). A Brief History of Stigmergy. Artificial Life, 5(2), 97–116. doi:10.1162/106454699568700. PMID 10633572. This paper formalized the definition: stigmergy is 'a mechanism of indirect coordination, through the environment, between agents or actions,' where 'the trace left in the environment by an individual action stimulates the performance of a succeeding action by the same or different agent.' Notably the paper does NOT itself use the phrase 'external memory' or 'collective memory' as technical terms, but it establishes the mechanism that later reviewers describe that way.
findings.citation: Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (1999). A Brief History of Stigmergy. Artificial Life, 5(2), 97–116. doi:10.1162/106454699568700. PMID 10633572. Confirmed via MIT Press direct listing (direct.mit.edu/artl/article/5/2/97/2318), PubMed, and ACM DL (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1162/106454699568700).

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — trail pheromone persistence and decay timescales (ants)
findings.claim: Jeanson, Ratnieks & Deneubourg (2003) measured trail pheromone decay in Pharaoh's ant (Monomorium pharaonis): half-life ~9 min on polycarbonate plastic and ~3 min on paper substrate, measured behaviorally (50% trail following vs. 80–70% at t=0). For Linepithema humile (Argentine ant), the synthetic trail pheromone (Z)-9-hexadecenal has an estimated half-life of ~30 min. Beckers et al. estimated Lasius niger trail lifetime at ~47 min. These values are substrate- and species-dependent and range from minutes to less than one hour — establishing a clear separation from direct-contact (sub-second) channels by 2–4 orders of magnitude.
findings.citation: Jeanson, R., Ratnieks, F.L.W. & Deneubourg, J.L. (2003). Pheromone trail decay rates on different substrates in the Pharaoh's ant, Monomorium pharaonis. Physiological Entomology, 28(3), 192–198. doi:10.1046/j.1365-3032.2003.00332.x. Linepithema ~30 min: reported in Deneubourg et al. self-organizing ant pattern studies; Lasius ~47 min: Beckers et al. cited in multiple review sources. FLAG: the Lasius 47 min value and Linepithema 30 min value were recovered from secondary review text, not from direct-fetched primary papers; treat as indicative but not fully attested.

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — trail pheromone reinforcement dynamics
findings.claim: Deneubourg and Goss (1989) demonstrated in Linepithema humile that when ants face a path bifurcation, positive feedback (more ants on a path → more pheromone deposited → more ants attracted) leads the colony to collectively select the shorter path. This self-amplifying loop is the core stigmergic optimization mechanism. Evaporation (the decay mechanism) is the essential counterweight: without pheromone decay, the colony cannot update to changed conditions. Decay therefore implements a 'forgetting function' — old information is automatically erased as new paths become more strongly marked.
findings.citation: Deneubourg, J.L. & Goss, S. (1989). Collective patterns and decision making. Ethology, Ecology & Evolution, 1(4), 295–311. doi:10.1080/08927014.1989.9525500. 'Self-organised shortcuts in the Argentine ant.' Naturwissenschaften, 76(12), 579–581. doi:10.1007/BF00374424. FLAG: both DOIs confirmed via search listings but not direct-fetched.

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — nest construction as environmentally stored template
findings.claim: In termite mound construction and ant nest architecture, the built structure itself functions as an environmental template that guides subsequent construction: the geometry of a growing pillar stimulates deposition at its tip, and spatial gradients in pheromone concentration on the structure encode the 'next step.' Turner (2000) and subsequent work on termite nest thermoregulation argue the nest is a physiological extension of the colony — an 'extended phenotype' in Dawkins' (1982) sense. A 2019 Insectes Sociaux paper (Theraulaz et al.) explicitly frames the nest as the extended phenotype of the colony as a whole, not of any one individual, emerging from stigmergic building rules.
findings.citation: Theraulaz et al. (2019). Deconstructing collective building in social insects: implications for ecological adaptation and evolution. Insectes Sociaux, 67, 5–20. doi:10.1007/s00040-019-00719-7. Confirmed via Springer Nature Link search result listing. FLAG: article content not directly fetched; citation confirmed from search metadata only.

findings.item: Low-speed stigmergic channel — queen pheromone and cuticular-hydrocarbon colony identity field
findings.claim: In ants, termites, and honeybees, cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) serve as persistent colony-identity signals, transferred between nestmates via trophallaxis and allogrooming, and also deposited on nest substrate (the 'gestalt odor' model). In Reticulitermes flavipes termites, the royal pheromone heneicosane (a CHC) was identified as a queen recognition signal: when applied to glass dummies it elicited worker behavioral responses identical to those of live queens (PNAS 2018). CHCs are long-chain waxy compounds with persistence timescales of hours to days on substrate surfaces (unlike volatile alarm pheromones). These form a colony-wide chemical identity field that is both written by colony members (via contact deposition) and read back by all colony members on each encounter. Whether this constitutes 'memory' in a technical sense is not established in the cited primary literature; it is better described as a persistent signal field.
findings.citation: Choe, D.H. et al. (2018). Identification of a queen and king recognition pheromone in the subterranean termite Reticulitermes flavipes. PNAS, 115(16), 4135–4140. doi:10.1073/pnas.1721419115. PMC5899469. PMID 29555778. Verified via direct PMC listing. Annual Reviews (2024): The Evolution of Queen Pheromone Production — doi:10.1146/annurev-ento-022124-124437 (confirmed from search listing; not directly fetched).

findings.item: Stigmergy as externalized environmental memory — establishment vs. metaphor
findings.claim: The framing of stigmergic traces as 'external memory' or 'collective memory' is found across the literature but with varying degrees of technical commitment. (A) Established mechanism: it is established (Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999; Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz 1999) that information generated by one individual's action is stored in the environment and read back by a different individual at a later time — this is the mechanism, not a metaphor. (B) Terminological framing: the terms 'collective memory,' 'external memory,' and 'extended cognition' (Clark & Chalmers 1998 extended-mind thesis) are applied to stigmergy by reviewers including Heylighen (Substack 2021+), and appear in the Wikipedia Stigmergy article as paraphrases of the mechanism, but are NOT used as technical terms in Grassé 1959 or Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999 themselves. (C) Niche-construction / ecological-inheritance framing: Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman's niche-construction theory recognizes colonial nest structures as 'ecological inheritance' — modifications of the environment that act as a second inheritance channel. This framing is documented in the primary niche-construction literature. VERDICT: the mechanism (environment stores information written by one agent, read later by others) is established; the labeling of that mechanism as 'memory' or 'cognition' is a researcher's interpretive framing, variably used in the literature, not a uniform technical consensus.
findings.citation: Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (1999). doi:10.1162/106454699568700. Bonabeau, E., Dorigo, M. & Theraulaz, G. (1999). Swarm Intelligence: From Natural to Artificial Systems. Oxford University Press. ISBN 0-19-513159-2. doi:10.1093/oso/9780195131581.001.0001. Niche construction: Odling-Smee, F.J., Laland, K.N. & Feldman, M.W. (2003). Niche Construction: The Neglected Process in Evolution. Princeton University Press. ISBN 978-0-691-04438-2. Ecological inheritance text confirmed via Springer review listing.

findings.item: Alarm propagation speed in ants — contact-mediated high-speed channel
findings.claim: Guo et al. (2022) used automated tracking + machine learning in seed-harvester ants: 39 of 46 ants transitioned to alarmed state within 1.51 ± 0.10 s after contact-mediated alarm stimulation. 83% of successful alarm transmissions occurred via direct physical contact; ~17% via independent excitement (likely pheromone diffusion without contact). The alarm wave shows rapid initial spread followed by precipitous decline — a transient burst pattern consistent with a high-speed channel rather than a persistent stored signal.
findings.citation: Guo, X., Lin, M.R., Azizi, A. et al. (2022). Decoding alarm signal propagation of seed-harvester ants using automated movement tracking and supervised machine learning. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 289(1967), 20212176. doi:10.1098/rspb.2021.2176. PMC8790334. Verified by direct PMC full-text fetch.

findings.item: Comparative synthesis — two-channel organization: how cleanly it separates in each taxon
findings.claim: ANTS: The two-channel split (sub-second contact ↔ minutes-to-hours pheromone trail) is the most cleanly separated of the three taxa in the documented literature. Direct contact (antennation: 19.5–41.5 strikes/s; alarm propagation: ~1.51 s via contact) vs. trail pheromone (half-life 3–47 min, species/substrate dependent) represent a 2–4 order-of-magnitude latency gap. The Deneubourg-Goss body of work provides the most quantified stigmergic dynamics. TERMITES: The split is also clean but asymmetric: vibrational alarm is ultra-fast (sub-second individual response, ~1.3 m/s propagation chain), while nest construction is among the most architecturally complex stigmergic stores known. However, termite pheromone trails and nest-construction pheromone persistence quantification is less precisely measured in the directly-verified literature than for ants. HONEYBEES: The two-channel framing is LEAST clean in honeybees. The waggle dance is a genuine edge case: it is a high-speed, direct, point-to-small-group kinematic signal that nonetheless encodes persistent spatial information (a distant resource vector). It is NOT stigmergic (the information is not stored in the environment), but it transfers ENVIRONMENTAL-SCALE information (location of a resource kilometers away) through a direct-contact channel. The stop signal (one-way, sub-second) is clearly the high-speed direct channel. Trail pheromones are used by stingless bees (Meliponini) but not by Apis mellifera, which instead relies on the waggle dance + volatile recruitment pheromones — reducing the stigmergic channel's role compared to ants. VERDICT: Ants > Termites > Honeybees in cleanness of the two-channel split. The waggle dance is the clearest documented case where the two-channel framing is the researcher's analytic frame, not a clean biological boundary.
findings.citation: Comparative framing synthesized from: Hager & Kirchner 2013 (termite vibration; doi:10.1242/jeb.086991); Jeanson et al. 2003 (ant trail; doi:10.1046/j.1365-3032.2003.00332.x); Tan et al. 2016 (stop signal; doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002423); von Frisch 1967 / Riley et al. 2005 (waggle dance). Stingless bee trail pheromones: Nieh, J.C. (2004). Recruitment communication in stingless bees. Apidologie, 35(2), 159–182. doi:10.1051/apido:2004007. FLAG: Nieh 2004 DOI confirmed from search listing; not directly fetched.

sonnet_survey.cross_cutting:
VERIFIED TWO-CHANNEL ORGANIZATION — SUMMARY

The literature establishes a genuine and robust two-channel communication organization in eusocial insect colonies, differing in latency by 2–4 orders of magnitude:

CHANNEL 1 — HIGH-SPEED / DIRECT / TRANSIENT (sub-second to seconds):
Antennation (19.5–41.5 strikes/s; reciprocal / bidirectional; O'Fallon et al. 2016, doi:10.1007/s00040-016-0462-6), trophallaxis (seconds-to-minutes per event; compound chemical signals including JH, CHCs, miRNA; LeBoeuf et al. 2016, doi:10.7554/eLife.20375), termite vibrational relay alarm (~0.3 s individual response time; Hager & Kirchner 2013, doi:10.1242/jeb.086991), honeybee stop signal (~150–258 ms pulses at 302–550 Hz; one-way inhibitory; Tan et al. 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002423), ant alarm propagation (1.51 ± 0.10 s via contact; 83% contact-mediated; Guo et al. 2022, doi:10.1098/rspb.2021.2176).

CHANNEL 2 — LOW-SPEED / STIGMERGIC / PERSISTENT (minutes to hours/days):
Trail pheromones (half-life 3–47 min depending on species and substrate; Jeanson et al. 2003, doi:10.1046/j.1365-3032.2003.00332.x), nest construction as environmental template (Grassé 1959, Insectes Sociaux 6:41–81; Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999, doi:10.1162/106454699568700), cuticular hydrocarbon identity fields on nest substrate (persistence hours to days; Choe et al. 2018, doi:10.1073/pnas.1721419115).

THE LOAD-BEARING FINDING ON STIGMERGY AS ENVIRONMENTAL STORE:
The mechanism — that information produced by one individual's action is deposited into the shared medium and read back by a different individual displaced in time — is established as the mechanism of stigmergy in primary literature (Grassé 1959; Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999; Bonabeau et al. 1999 Swarm Intelligence, ISBN 0-19-513159-2). The further framing of this as 'external memory,' 'collective memory,' or 'extended cognition' is an interpretive overlay applied by reviewers (Heylighen; Wikipedia Stigmergy article) but is not a technical consensus term in the primary behavioral-ecology literature. The niche-construction framing (Odling-Smee et al. 2003) provides the closest formal theoretical treatment of the built structure as an environmentally-stored inheritance channel.

FRAMEWORK LENS (offered as a lens only; not attributed to any cited author):
Reading the colony as a distributed store/retrieve system — the direct-contact channel as the transient reciprocal edge between air-gapped bodies, and the stigmergic channel as a persistent WRITE/READ store externalized into the shared medium (sculpt/deposit = write; follow/respond = read) — is a reading the cited behavioral ecology literature supports mechanistically, though none of the cited authors frame it in these terms. This is the researcher's (or analyst's) framing applied to attested mechanisms, not a claim the cited authors make. The colony is, observationally, the most human-latency and directly-observable instance of this kind of distributed information architecture — mechanisms that cellular substrates run at timescales far below human perception are here slowed to watchable and measurable timescales.
sonnet_survey.uncentered_note: The two-channel framing is cleanest for ants, where the latency gap between direct contact (sub-second) and pheromone trail (minutes) is most quantified in the primary literature. For termites, the vibrational alarm channel is well-attested but pheromone-trail and construction-pheromone persistence data are less precisely quantified in directly-verified sources. For honeybees, the waggle dance is a genuine boundary case that defies clean two-channel assignment: it encodes persistent spatial information (characteristic of the stigmergic channel) via a transient direct-contact mechanism (characteristic of the fast channel). This is not a defect of the biology; it is the honeybee's evolutionary solution to the problem of encoding spatial vectors across a volatile medium without a substrate to mark. The two-channel framing is therefore partially a researcher's analytic imposition when applied to Apis mellifera, and the literature does not uniformly apply this framing — it is the task description's lens, not the field's consensus organizing principle. The superorganism concept itself remains contested at the evolutionary-mechanism level (kin selection vs. multi-level selection), though the descriptive colony-as-organism framing is broadly accepted for functional analysis.

merged_findings.claim: The concept that a eusocial colony functions as one integrated organism — with the reproductive caste as germ-line and workers/soldiers as differentiated soma — was articulated by William Morton Wheeler in 'The ant-colony as an organism' (1911). Wheeler treated the colony, not the individual ant, as the analog of the organism: it acts as a cohesive unit, persists, develops, and reproduces as a unit.
merged_findings.best_citation: Wheeler, W.M. (1911). The ant-colony as an organism. Journal of Morphology 22(2):307-325. No DOI (1911 paper); bibliographic details corroborated across AntCat (ref 130060), PsycNET (record 1911-10101-003), and J. Morphol. vol. 22 contents.

merged_findings.item: 1. SUPERORGANISM — modern synthesis (Hoelldobler & Wilson 2009) + colony/hive terminology
merged_findings.claim: The superorganism framing received its definitive modern sociobiological synthesis in Hoelldobler & Wilson, 'The Superorganism' (2009), framing the colony as an integrated organism whose organization emerges from local-interaction feedback rather than hierarchical command. TERMINOLOGY (verified consistent with the cited literature): 'colony' / 'superorganism' = the distributed organismal unit (ants, termites, bees); 'hive' = the honey-bee NEST structure (physical domicile) specifically, never the organism and not used for ants/termites. Same authors wrote 'The Ants' (1990, Harvard/Springer, 732 pp), a primary ant-communication reference.
merged_findings.best_citation: Hoelldobler, B. & Wilson, E.O. (2009). The Superorganism: The Beauty, Elegance, and Strangeness of Insect Societies. W.W. Norton, New York. ISBN 978-0-393-06704-0. Verified via Norton publisher page + QRB review (DOI 10.1086/650272). Colony-vs-hive usage standard in von Frisch / Seeley / Hoelldobler & Wilson.

merged_findings.claim: The superorganism framing is widely USED as an organizing heuristic but is CONTESTED as a strict evolutionary entity-level claim. It declined post-1960s with gene-centered / kin-selection thinking and revived with multi-level selection. Gardner & Grafen (2009) gave the first formal theory of group adaptation, concluding genuine superorganism-grade group adaptation arises only under restrictive conditions (effectively clonal/maximally-related groups; conflict-suppression like policing is NOT itself a group adaptation). Boomsma & Gawne (2018) argue the loose ('sensu lato') concept is uninformative and restrict true superorganismality to lineages with irreversible morphological caste differentiation (a 'point of no return' tied to lifetime monogamy / high relatedness). The Nowak-Tarnita-Wilson (2010) attack on inclusive-fitness theory (and the 130+ author rebuttal, Nature 471:E1-E4, 2011) is the backdrop, but that debate concerns the evolutionary ORIGIN of eusociality, not the descriptive colony-as-organism framing.
merged_findings.best_citation: Gardner, A. & Grafen, A. (2009). Capturing the superorganism: a formal theory of group adaptation. J. Evol. Biol. 22(4):659-671. DOI 10.1111/j.1420-9101.2008.01681.x, PMID 19210588 (verified Oxford Academic/PubMed). Boomsma, J.J. & Gawne, R. (2018). Superorganismality and caste differentiation as points of no return. Biol. Rev. 93(1):28-54. DOI 10.1111/brv.12330, PMID 28508537 (verified Wiley/PubMed). Backdrop: Nowak, M.A., Tarnita, C.E. & Wilson, E.O. (2010). The evolution of eusociality. Nature 466:1057-1062. DOI 10.1038/nature09205 (paywalled at Nature; OA via Princeton institutional repository — attestable via the OA chain; not direct-fetched this pass).

merged_findings.item: 1b. SUPERORGANISM — organizational-approach critique (Canciani, Arnellos & Moreno 2019) [CORRECTED ATTRIBUTION]
merged_findings.claim: A 2019 Frontiers in Psychology review revisits the superorganism via an organizational (autonomy/individuality) approach to complex eusociality, and notes that the mainstream framing — that hierarchical control does not occur — may underweight Wheeler's original physiological emphasis. NOTE: this finding originated in the sonnet survey under a FALSE author attribution (Witkowski & Ikegami); the actual authors are Canciani, Arnellos & Moreno. Carried in CORRECTED.
merged_findings.best_citation: Canciani, M., Arnellos, A. & Moreno, A. (2019). Revising the Superorganism: An Organizational Approach to Complex Eusociality. Frontiers in Psychology 10:2653. DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02653, PMC6901679, PMID 31849768. Authors verified via Frontiers + PMC + PubMed + Semantic Scholar.

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — antennation (rate, timescale, bidirectionality) [CORRECTED PAGINATION]
merged_findings.claim: Antennation is direct antenna-to-body contact between adjacent individuals; it is the read step for cuticular-hydrocarbon (CHC) nestmate-recognition and task-allocation cues, sub-second-to-seconds and transient. It is RECIPROCAL/bidirectional as mutual physical assay (both ants drum each other's antennae simultaneously or in rapid alternation). O'Fallon et al. (2016) measured 19.5-41.5 antenna strikes/s in Odontomachus trap-jaw ants by high-speed videography — so fast it is invisible to the unaided eye. Colony-wide contact rates oscillate (~3-4 peaks/hr), shaping information transmission (Richardson et al. 2017). NOTE: sonnet cited O'Fallon as 63(3):409-417; CORRECTED to 63(2):265-270.
merged_findings.best_citation: O'Fallon, S., Suarez, A.V. & Smith, A.A. (2016). A comparative analysis of rapid antennation behavior in four species of Odontomachus trap-jaw ants. Insectes Sociaux 63(2):265-270. DOI 10.1007/s00040-016-0462-6 (issue+pages CORRECTED, verified Springer). Contact-rate oscillation: Richardson, T.O. et al. (2017). Short-term activity cycles impede information transmission in ant colonies. PLOS Comput. Biol. 13(5):e1005527, DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005527, PMC5443549.

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — trophallaxis (fluid exchange carrying chemical + information)
merged_findings.claim: Trophallaxis is mouth-to-mouth (stomodeal) fluid exchange between adjacent individuals — direct, contact-based, seconds-to-minutes per event (Greenwald et al. 2015 report mean inter-event interval ~240+/-17 s in Camponotus). LeBoeuf et al. (2016) showed the exchanged oral fluid in the ANT Camponotus floridanus carries far more than food — specific proteins, hydrocarbons, microRNAs, and juvenile hormone (JH) — constituting a private, colony-spanning chemical-information network influencing collective development (JH-supplemented workers reared larvae ~2x as likely to complete metamorphosis). Antennation accompanies the exchange (bidirectional in the signaling layer) even when food flow is one-directional; rare donor<->receiver role reversals confirm it is not strictly unidirectional. NOTE: the task framed trophallaxis with honeybees, but the JH/protein/miRNA payload finding is attributed to the ant.
merged_findings.best_citation: LeBoeuf, A.C. et al. (2016). Oral transfer of chemical cues, growth proteins and hormones in social insects. eLife 5:e20375. DOI 10.7554/eLife.20375, PMID 27894417, PMC5153251 (verified eLife/PubMed; species = Camponotus floridanus). Trophallactic-network timing: Greenwald, E., Segre, E. & Feinerman, O. (2015). Ant trophallactic networks: simultaneous measurement of interaction patterns and food dissemination. Sci. Rep. 5:12496. DOI 10.1038/srep12496, PMID 26224025, PMC4519732 (verified).

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — termite vibrational / substrate-borne alarm (head-banging, relay) [DOI CORRECTED]
merged_findings.claim: Disturbed termite soldiers (and workers) drum the head against the substrate, producing pulse-train substrate-borne vibrational ALARM signals (~10-26 Hz; M. subhyalinus ~13 Hz, M. bellicosus ~26 Hz). In Macrotermes natalensis pulse-trains propagate at ~130 m/s along nest galleries (attenuating ~0.4 dB/cm; direct-wave range ~0.4 m per source). Individual soldiers respond within ~0.3 s by themselves drumming, creating RELAY chains that propagate alarm colony-wide at ~1.3 m/s (M. natalensis) to ~2.1 m/s (Odontotermes sp.) without decrement. The relay (receivers re-drum) is the clearest documented positive-feedback/closed-loop relay structure in this catalog, though the net propagation is broadcast (alarm->flee/attack), not a targeted dialogue. NOTE: opus cited DOI 10.1242/jeb.083295; CORRECTED to 10.1242/jeb.086991 (sonnet had this right).
merged_findings.best_citation: Hager, F.A. & Kirchner, W.H. (2013). Vibrational long-distance communication in the termites Macrotermes natalensis and Odontotermes sp. J. Exp. Biol. 216(17):3249-3256. DOI 10.1242/jeb.086991 (CORRECTED), PMID 23926309 (verified at journals.biologists.com).

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — honeybee stop-signal (inhibitory, answered) + DVAV vibration signal
merged_findings.claim: The honeybee STOP-signal is a brief vibrational pulse (~302-550 Hz, ~150-258 ms/pulse) delivered by head-butting a waggle-dancer or departing forager, halting/inhibiting her — an explicitly directed, signal-elicits-response interaction (receiver freezes during delivery). Tan et al. (2016, in Apis cerana) showed it encodes graded danger: frequency rises with threat severity (~550 Hz/~258 ms in nest-attack vs ~502 Hz/~178 ms in forager-attack contexts) and serves both foraging inhibition and colony alarm. Nieh (2010) earlier showed foragers meeting peril deliver stop-signals to dancers advertising that site (negative feedback curbing recruitment). The DVAV/vibration ('shaking') signal (~18 Hz, ~1-1.4 s bouts) non-specifically raises recipient activity. The stop-signal is the cleanest 'closed-loop edge' in the bee literature; it is delivered one-to-one and receivers do not reciprocate with their own stop-signals.
merged_findings.best_citation: Tan, K. et al. (2016). Honey Bee Inhibitory Signaling Is Tuned to Threat Severity and Can Act as a Colony Alarm Signal. PLOS Biology 14(3):e1002423. DOI 10.1371/journal.pbio.1002423, PMID 27014876, PMC4807812 (verified; species Apis cerana). Negative-feedback stop-signal: Nieh, J.C. (2010). Current Biology 20(4):310-315, DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2009.12.060 (verified). DVAV freq/duration: long-term DVAV characterization (Sci. Rep. 2018, PMC6167329).

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — fast volatile alarm pheromones (rapid release; decay NOT quantified)
merged_findings.claim: Isoamyl (isopentyl) acetate (IPA) is the principal sting-alarm pheromone component in Apis mellifera (Boch, Shearer & Stone 1962), synthesized near the sting (Koschevnikov gland), highly volatile, rapidly released on disturbance to trigger fast defensive recruitment. Ant alarm pheromones (e.g. fire-ant Solenopsis invicta alkylpyrazines from mandibular glands) act similarly at seconds-to-minutes before the active concentration drops below threshold. The channel is near-instantaneous, transient, broadcast-to-nearby-nestmates, largely ONE-WAY release-and-amplify (responders may release their own pheromone -> positive-feedback amplification, not a targeted reply). FLAG: a quantified DECAY/half-life IN SECONDS for IPA / fire-ant alarm pheromone was NOT pinned to a directly-fetched primary source in either run; the classical active-space kinetics reference is Bossert & Wilson 1963 (not fetched). The identity + high volatility are well-established; the 'rapid decay quantified' claim is qualitatively asserted, not quantitatively attested.
merged_findings.best_citation: Boch, R., Shearer, D.A. & Stone, B.C. (1962). Identification of iso-amyl acetate as an active component in the sting pheromone of the honey bee. Nature 195:1018-1020. DOI 10.1038/1951018b0 (verified at source this pass via ADS bibcode 1962Natur.195.1018B + nature.com/articles/1951018b0 — upgrades both runs' 'not reverified' status). Quantified decay: UNATTESTED (Bossert & Wilson 1963 active-space model not fetched).

merged_findings.item: 2. HIGH-SPEED CHANNEL — ant alarm propagation (contact-mediated, transient burst)
merged_findings.claim: Guo et al. (2022) used automated tracking + supervised machine learning in seed-harvester ants (Pogonomyrmex californicus): after alarming three ants, 39 of 46 transitioned to alarmed state within 1.51+/-0.10 s of contact-mediated stimulation; ~83% of successful transmissions were via direct physical contact, ~17% via independent excitement (likely pheromone diffusion). The alarm wave shows rapid spread then precipitous decline — a transient burst consistent with a high-speed channel rather than a persistent stored signal. (Sonnet-only finding; pulled in.)
merged_findings.best_citation: Guo, X. et al. (2022). Decoding alarm signal propagation of seed-harvester ants using automated movement tracking and supervised machine learning. Proc. R. Soc. B 289(1967):20212176. DOI 10.1098/rspb.2021.2176, PMID 35078355, PMC8790334 (verified; species Pogonomyrmex californicus).

merged_findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — trail pheromones (deposition, persistence/half-life, reinforcement)
merged_findings.claim: Trail pheromones are deposited on the substrate (WRITTEN) and FOLLOWED later (READ), persisting minutes-to-much-longer with positive-feedback reinforcement (more traffic -> more deposition -> stronger trail) and negative-feedback / no-entry signals. Persistence is highly species- and substrate-dependent: Pharaoh ant (Monomorium pharaonis) trail half-life ~9 min on polycarbonate, ~3 min on paper (~50% efficacy loss in ~3 min on paper; Jeanson et al. 2003); Argentine ant (Linepithema humile) synthetic trail ~30 min; Lasius niger ~47 min (Beckers et al.); Oecophylla longinoda marks remained detectable for weeks. Czaczkes, Gruter & Ratnieks (2015) give the integrative review: trails regulate foraging via positive AND negative feedback, complementary with individual memory. FLAG: the Linepithema ~30 min and Lasius ~47 min values were recovered from secondary review text in the sonnet run, not direct-fetched primary papers — indicative, not fully attested.
merged_findings.best_citation: Czaczkes, T.J., Gruter, C. & Ratnieks, F.L.W. (2015). Trail pheromones: an integrative view of their role in social insect colony organization. Annu. Rev. Entomol. 60:581-599. DOI 10.1146/annurev-ento-010814-020627, PMID 25386724 (verified). Pharaoh-ant decay: Jeanson, R., Ratnieks, F.L.W. & Deneubourg, J.-L. (2003). Physiol. Entomol. 28(3):192-198, DOI 10.1046/j.1365-3032.2003.00332.x (verified). Linepithema/Lasius values: secondary-review only (FLAG).

merged_findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — trail-pheromone reinforcement / decay-as-forgetting dynamics
merged_findings.claim: Deneubourg & Goss (1989) and the classic Argentine-ant shortcut experiment showed that at a path bifurcation positive feedback (more ants -> more pheromone -> more ants) leads the colony to collectively select the shorter path; evaporation (decay) is the essential counterweight implementing a 'forgetting function' so the colony can update to changed conditions. This is the core stigmergic optimization mechanism. FLAG: both DOIs were confirmed from search listings in the sonnet run, not direct-fetched this pass. (Sonnet-only finding; pulled in.)
merged_findings.best_citation: Deneubourg, J.L. & Goss, S. (1989). Collective patterns and decision making. Ethology, Ecology & Evolution 1(4):295-311. DOI 10.1080/08927014.1989.9525500. 'Self-organised shortcuts in the Argentine ant.' Naturwissenschaften 76(12):579-581. DOI 10.1007/BF00374424. (Both confirmed via search listing; not direct-fetched — FLAG.)

merged_findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — STIGMERGY as organizing principle (Grasse 1959; Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999)
merged_findings.claim: Grasse (1959) coined 'stigmergie' from termite nest-(re)construction in Bellicositermes natalensis and Cubitermes sp.: the work already accomplished (a soil pellet, a pillar) stimulates the next act, so coordination is mediated by the modified ENVIRONMENT, not by direct worker-to-worker instruction — termites respond to the structure already built, with no individual holding a blueprint. Theraulaz & Bonabeau (1999) formalized it ('indirect coordination, through the environment, between agents or actions') and distinguished quantitative vs qualitative stigmergy. It is the LOW-SPEED, INDIRECT, environment-mediated, one-to-many-across-time channel. NOTE: Theraulaz & Bonabeau (1999) does NOT itself use 'external/collective memory' as technical terms — it establishes the mechanism later reviewers describe that way.
merged_findings.best_citation: Grasse, P.-P. (1959). La reconstruction du nid et les coordinations interindividuelles chez Bellicositermes natalensis et Cubitermes sp. La theorie de la stigmergie. Insectes Sociaux 6(1):41-80. DOI 10.1007/BF02223791 (verified Springer/Semantic Scholar; end-page 80 vs 81 minor index ambiguity). Theraulaz, G. & Bonabeau, E. (1999). A brief history of stigmergy. Artificial Life 5(2):97-116. DOI 10.1162/106454699568700, PMID 10633572 (verified MIT Press/PubMed).

merged_findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — nest/structure as environmentally-stored template; built structure as extended phenotype
merged_findings.claim: Built nest structures are environmentally-stored templates: the partially-built structure (geometry of a growing pillar; spatial pheromone gradients on it) encodes the next builder's action, persisting hours-to-days-to-the-colony-lifetime. Turner (2000) and subsequent work frame the termite nest as a physiological extension of the colony — an 'extended phenotype' (Dawkins 1982) of the colony as a whole, emerging from stigmergic building rules. FLAG: the Theraulaz et al. 2019 Insectes Sociaux 'deconstructing collective building' paper (DOI 10.1007/s00040-019-00719-7) and termite construction-pheromone persistence figures were confirmed from search metadata only in the sonnet run, not direct-fetched.
merged_findings.best_citation: Stigmergic-construction templates: Camazine, S. et al. (2001). Self-Organization in Biological Systems. Princeton Univ. Press. ISBN 978-0-691-11624-2 (canonical reference, not re-verified at source this pass). Extended-phenotype framing: Theraulaz et al. (2019). Deconstructing collective building in social insects. Insectes Sociaux, DOI 10.1007/s00040-019-00719-7 (search-metadata only — FLAG).

merged_findings.item: 3. LOW-SPEED CHANNEL — queen pheromone & cuticular-hydrocarbon (CHC) colony-identity field
merged_findings.claim: In ants, termites, and honeybees, cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) form a persistent colony-IDENTITY field (the 'gestalt odor'), transferred between nestmates via trophallaxis/allogrooming and deposited on nest substrate (persistence hours-to-days, unlike volatile alarm pheromones). Recognition cues can be deposited INTO and re-acquired FROM shared nest material itself (nest soil mediates indirect transfer of recognition cues between nestmates) — a stigmergic identity-field mechanism. In Reticulitermes flavipes termites the royal pheromone heneicosane (a CHC) was identified as a queen/king recognition signal: applied to glass dummies it elicited worker responses identical to live royals (Choe et al. 2018). Whether this constitutes 'memory' technically is not established in the primary literature; it is best described as a persistent signal field.
merged_findings.best_citation: Termite royal pheromone: Choe, D.H. et al. (2018). Identification of a queen and king recognition pheromone in the subterranean termite Reticulitermes flavipes. PNAS 115(16):4135-4140. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1721419115, PMID 29555778, PMC5899469 (verified PMC). Nest-material recognition-cue transfer: 'Wax On, Wax Off: Nest Soil Facilitates Indirect Transfer of Recognition Cues' (PLoS ONE, PMC3084846, verified).

merged_findings.item: 3. LOAD-BEARING QUESTION — is stigmergy treated as EXTERNALIZED, ENVIRONMENTALLY-STORED MEMORY?
merged_findings.claim: YES at the MECHANISM level, with the 'memory' LABEL graded. (A) MECHANISM — established: information produced by one individual's action is deposited into the shared medium and read back by a different individual displaced in time (Grasse 1959; Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999; Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz 1999). (B) OPERATIONAL 'external memory' — Hunt, Franks & Baddeley (2020) state it plainly: 'store the information externally in the environment'; treat the shared substrate as an 'external memory store'; Temnothorax albipennis ants converge on optimal exploration faster when prior chemical marks accumulate (uncleaned arena, p=0.0161) — framing the colony as a Bayesian superorganism. So 'collective/external/stigmergic memory' IS an established, operationally-defined usage in this primary source. (C) METAPHORICAL extension — 'extended cognition / extended mind' (Clark & Chalmers 1998) and the niche-construction 'ecological inheritance' framing (Odling-Smee et al. 2003) are interpretive overlays, NOT technical terms in Grasse 1959 or Theraulaz & Bonabeau 1999, and not a uniform technical consensus.
